author: Tabbo2
quote:
When a game already holds a permanent spot in the pantheon of gaming history, the prospect of a full-scale remake carries an immense weight. How do you modernize a foundational masterpiece without losing the magic that made it legendary in the first place? With the 2026 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Nintendo Switch 2, Nintendo hasn't just answered that question—they have delivered the definitive way to experience the greatest adventure ever told. Giving this a 10 out of 10 feels less like a generous rating and more like an inevitability.

From the very first moment you step out of Kokiri Forest onto a sunlit Hyrule Field, it is unmistakably clear this is far more than a simple coat of fresh paint. Built from the ground up for the Switch 2, the visual overhaul is breathtaking. Every texture tells a story, from the handwoven threads of Link's tunic to the weathered stone of the Temple of Time and the vibrant, bustling streets of Hyrule Castle Town—which now replaces the static painted backdrops of 1998 with living, breathing 3D architecture. Running at a locked 60 frames per second with near-instantaneous load times, Hyrule feels cohesive, tactile, and astonishingly alive. Crucially, Nintendo preserved the iconic art direction and atmospheric lighting that gave the original its unmistakable fairytale-meets-dark-fantasy tone, ensuring that moments like stepping into the ruined Market as Adult Link feel just as haunting as they did decades ago.

Where this remake truly shines, however, is in how thoughtfully it elevates the gameplay for modern players without sandblasting away its identity. Full free-camera control, crisp gyro-assisted aiming for the Fairy Bow and Hookshot, and a smoother dodge-and-dash system make combat and traversal feel remarkably snappy and responsive. Even the addition of a manual jump button—carefully integrated alongside subtly reworked environmental geometry—adds a newfound sense of agility without breaking classic dungeon progression. Quality-of-life upgrades abound: the inventory is cleanly organized across Child, Adult, and combined tabs; Navi's interruptions are now unobtrusive silent text bubbles; an accessible songbook keeps your ocarina melodies handy; and the new "Threads of Time" tracker helps players keep tabs on side quests and story beats without ever holding your hand too tightly. Even subtle refinements, like real-time Din's Fire casting, five bottle slots, and a starting wallet of 200 rupees, eliminate dated friction while keeping the core challenge intact.

The dungeon design remains an absolute masterclass in pacing, spatial awareness, and atmospheric storytelling. From the eerie verticality of the Forest Temple to the fiery depths of the Fire Temple and the labyrinthine water-level puzzles of the Water Temple—now far less tedious thanks to streamlined equipment swapping—every temple feels like a cohesive, memorable trial. Longtime fans will also discover plenty of clever surprises tucked into every corner of the kingdom. Skulltulas sport updated attack patterns, the Forest Temple introduces smart puzzle adjustments that keep twenty-year veterans on their toes, and cracked ground tiles subtly telegraph hidden bombable grottos without ruining the thrill of discovery.

The audio presentation is nothing short of transcendent. Koji Kondo's legendary score has been re-recorded with a full symphonic orchestra, swelling dynamically as you gallop across the plains on Epona or descend into the chilling depths of the Shadow Temple. Every sword clash, ambient forest breeze, and echoing footstep has been painstakingly remastered. Full voice acting during key cutscenes—paired with expressive new character animations and expanded dialogue—brings tremendous emotional weight to Link's journey through time, making the tragedy of Hyrule's seven-year fall and the bonds with characters like Saria, Zelda, and Sheik hit harder than ever before.

Once you've conquered the main quest, the remake continues to reward curiosity. Hyrule Castle Town features new faces and charming side interactions, Kakariko Village offers a handy scarecrow training dummy, and the new "Hall of Fallen Foes" lets you rematch iconic bosses at will. Throw in playful touches like the Business Scrub Seed for summoning Deku merchants and optional microphone support to hum or whistle your own ocarina melodies, and it becomes obvious how much genuine care went into every detail.

Ultimately, what makes this remake a 10/10 triumph is its deep reverence for the source material. It understands that Ocarina of Time isn't merely a checklist of dungeons—it is a timeless coming-of-age odyssey about courage, memory, and the bittersweet passage of childhood. Whether you are drawing the Master Sword for the first time or returning to Hyrule nearly thirty years later, this remake captures lightning in a bottle all over again. It is pure, unadulterated magic, and an unforgettable achievement.
game_title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time

author: Tabbo2
quote:
The game has too much nudity and adding a female main character ruins the aurafarming that Jason does to make up for these graphics honestly very disappointing and underwhelming for 13 years of work you'd think they would put effort into this game, and speaking of the graphics, they are straight-up ass. Seriously, for a next-gen title with a massive budget, everything looks muddy, washed out, and outdated, like an early PS4 game upscaled with a blurry filter. The lighting is flat, reflections look pixelated and broken, character faces look like plastic mannequins with dead eyes, and the shadows flicker constantly whenever you move the camera. 

​The physics feel completely phoned in too. The driving mechanics lost all the weight and realism they used to have, making every car feel like a weightless arcade toy instead of an actual vehicle. You can slam into a concrete barrier at top speed and bounce off with barely a scratch, which completely ruins any sense of immersion. On top of that, the open world feels weirdly empty and lifeless compared to all the hype and trailers. Half the buildings you think you can enter are just painted-on textures and locked doors, and the NPC AI is somehow worse than games from over a decade ago. Pedestrians either stare blankly at walls or despawn the second you turn the camera around, making the city feel like a cheap movie set rather than a living, breathing environment.

​The mission design is painfully repetitive as well—just endless fetch quests, tedious driving segments, and slow tailing missions with zero creativity or freedom in how you complete them. If you step two feet outside the exact path the developers want you to take, you get an instant mission failed screen. For a modern open-world title, that kind of rigid hand-holding is embarrassing. Even the gunplay feels clunky and outdated, with awkward cover mechanics, terrible hit registration, and bullet-sponge enemies that take way too many hits to go down.

​Technical performance and glitches are by far the worst part of the entire experience. The game is practically held together with duct tape, with constant bugs completely breaking immersion every ten minutes. Cars randomly spawn inside each other and launch into the stratosphere, NPCs T-pose in the middle of serious cutscenes, and character models regularly clip straight through walls and floors. Mission triggers fail to activate constantly, forcing you to restart entire checkpoints from scratch because an AI partner got stuck on a curb or walked endlessly into a closed door. Falling through the map while driving is a regular occurrence, and saves can randomly corrupt or fail to load properly after a crash. On top of the glitches, the framerate tanks whenever you drive fast through the city or get into a big shootout, accompanied by jarring texture pop-in where roads and buildings turn into low-poly blobs right in front of your eyes, plus audio cutting out mid-dialogue. Waiting over thirteen years only to get a broken, choppy, unpolished mess is completely unacceptable. 

​Even the story pacing falls completely flat. The plot drags on for hours without anything meaningful happening, filled with forgettable side characters and forced dialogue that tries way too hard to be funny. The side activities feel like mindless filler copy-pasted across the map just to artificially pad out the runtime, offering zero worthwhile rewards for your time. Meanwhile, the in-game economy and progression system are clearly balanced to frustrate players rather than reward them, making basic upgrades, properties, and vehicles feel like an exhausting, tedious chore—obviously designed to push people toward spending extra money later on.

​Even the user interface and menus feel clunky, unresponsive, and poorly organized, making simple tasks like swapping gear, setting waypoints, or checking the map way more annoying than they should be. Sound design is underwhelming too, with weak weapon audio that sounds like airsoft guns and a radio soundtrack that lacks any real variety or memorable tracks. It honestly feels like the studio spent way more time and money on flashy marketing campaigns and CGI trailers than on actual gameplay depth, quality assurance, graphics, or innovation. Truly a massive letdown for the franchise and easily the most overrated, broken release of the year.
